writtenQuestions.text:
A lunar mission has recently brought samples from the Moon. The following experiments were then carried out on it. Point out the branch of chemistry these experiments are related to.

1. Determining its composition
2. Studying the physical properties of materials it contains
3. Carrying out chemical reactions with usual inorganic reagents
modelAnswer: 1. Determining the sample's composition involves analysis of its components, so it is analytical chemistry.
2. Studying physical properties of materials is related to physical chemistry.
3. Reactions with usual inorganic reagents are related to inorganic chemistry.
Therefore, the branches are analytical chemistry, physical chemistry and inorganic chemistry, respectively.

explain.title: What chemistry studies
explain.body: Chemistry is the branch of science which deals with the properties, composition and the structure of substances. It also deals with the physical and chemical changes in matter and the laws or principles which govern these changes.

explain.title: Why chemistry has branches
explain.body: Chemistry is a widely spread, complex subject. Its branches give scientists distinct areas to focus on, making it possible to study specific aspects and achieve breakthroughs and advancements.

explain.title: Physical and analytical chemistry
explain.body: Physical chemistry investigates how substances behave at atomic and molecular levels. Analytical chemistry deals with the analysis of substances through separation, identification and determination of component concentrations.

explain.title: Organic, inorganic and nuclear chemistry
explain.body: Organic chemistry deals with carbon compounds other than simple salts such as carbonates, bicarbonates, oxides and carbides. Inorganic chemistry studies elements and compounds that contain little or no carbon. Nuclear chemistry deals with reactions taking place in an atom's nucleus.

explain.title: Chemistry in living things, the environment and space
explain.body: Biochemistry studies chemical substances and vital processes in living organisms. Environmental chemistry studies chemical phenomena and species in air, soil and water. Astrochemistry studies molecules and ions in space and interstellar space.

mistakes: Mixing up analytical chemistry (analyzing components) with a branch that studies what substances do or how they behave.
Calling every study of a carbon-containing molecule biochemistry: organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, while biochemistry focuses on living organisms and their chemical processes.
Confusing inorganic chemistry with nuclear chemistry: inorganic chemistry concerns elements and compounds with little or no carbon; nuclear chemistry concerns reactions in atomic nuclei.
Giving only one reason when asked for three reasons chemistry is divided into branches.
Writing a branch name without linking it to the topic in a branch-identification question.

explain.title: What matter and a state of matter mean
explain.body: Your textbook defines matter as: “Anything other than energy which carries weight and occupies volume is called matter.” It defines a state of matter as: “A state of matter is one of the many distinct forms in which matter can exist.” The four states observed in everyday life are solid, liquid, gas and plasma.

explain.title: Solids, liquids and gases
explain.body: Solids have a definite shape and fixed volume; their particles are closely packed and can oscillate about their mean positions. Liquid molecules are closely attached but move randomly. Gas molecules are very widely apart, have no order whatsoever and have very weak intermolecular forces, so gases are easily compressible and have very low densities.

explain.title: Plasma and other states
explain.body: Your textbook defines plasma as: “Plasma can be considered as a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions, photons, etc.” It gives fluorescent tubes, lightning and welding arcs as examples. Supercritical fluids show properties of both gases and liquids. Liquid crystals have properties between conventional liquids and crystalline solids.

explain.title: Graphene and exotic states
explain.body: Graphene is a two-dimensional crystal: a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern. The section describes it as tough, flexible and light, with a high resistance. States not commonly encountered are called exotic states of matter; examples include dark matter and Bose-Einstein condensate.

Do not confuse graphene with liquid crystal: graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, while liquid crystal properties are between those of conventional liquids and crystalline solids.
When describing supercritical fluids, include both gas and liquid properties, not just one of them.

explain.title: Compound

explain.title: Mixture
explain.body: A mixture is formed when more than one types of elements or compounds are mixed together in any ratio. A mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

writtenQuestions.text: What are allotropic forms? Explain the allotropic forms of carbon and sulphur. How does coal differ from diamond?
modelAnswer: Allotropic forms are different structural forms of the same element.
Carbon has three main allotropic forms: diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene (C₆₀).
Diamond has a giant macromolecular structure.
Graphite has a layered structure of hexagonal rings of carbon.
Buckminster fullerene (C₆₀) consists of a cage-like sphere of atoms arranged in pentagons and hexagons.
Sulphur exists in two crystalline allotropic forms: rhombic and monoclinic sulphur.
Rhombic sulphur is more stable than monoclinic sulphur.
Coal is an impure, non-crystalline form of carbon, whereas diamond is a crystalline form of carbon with a giant macromolecular structure.

explain.title: Elements
explain.body: An element is the simplest form of matter. It is a pure substance containing the same kind of atoms. It is not possible to break down an element into simpler particles by ordinary chemical reactions.

explain.title: Compounds
explain.body: A compound is a pure substance. It is formed by the chemical combination of two or more atoms of different elements. In a compound, the atoms of elements must combine together by a fixed ratio by weight. A compound can be broken into its constituent elements by a chemical reaction.

explain.title: Mixtures

explain.body: A solution is such a mixture in which solute particles are completely homogenized in the solvent e.g. dissolution of sodium chloride or copper sulphate in water. explain.title: Suspension
explain.body: A suspension, on the other hand, is a mixture in which solute particles do not dissolve in the solvent. We can actually see these particles. If a suspension is kept for some time, these particles settle down. Again, if this suspension is filtered, the particles in it cannot pass through the pores of filter paper and can be collected as a residue. A mixture of chalk in water is an example of suspension.

explain.title: Colloidal solution
explain.body: Besides a true solution and a suspension, there is a third form of solution called colloidal solution. In this type, the solute particles do not homogenize with solvent. These particles are a little bit bigger than the solute particles present in the true solution but not big enough to be seen with a naked eye like the particles present in a suspension. If kept for some time, the particles of a colloidal solution do not settle down. On filtration, these particles pass through the filter paper like the particles of a true solution. Starch solution and white of an egg are the common examples of colloidal solutions.

mistakes: Do not say that colloidal particles settle; the section says they do not settle on standing.
Do not say colloidal particles are caught by filter paper; they pass through it.
Do not confuse a true solution with a colloid: both pass through filter paper, but colloidal particles are bigger than true-solution particles.
Do not use chalk in water as an example of a true solution; it is a suspension.

explain.title: Chemistry has branches
explain.body: Chemistry covers many substances, properties and reactions. Dividing it into branches makes its study organised and allows people to specialise. Each branch focuses on a different kind of question or material.

explain.title: Matter has different states and structures
explain.body: Matter includes solids, liquids and gases, as well as states such as plasma, liquid crystals and supercritical fluids. Elements can also occur in different structural forms called allotropes, such as diamond and graphite, which are both forms of carbon.

explain.title: Mixtures and solutions are different
explain.body: A true solution is uniform, while colloids and suspensions contain dispersed particles. A saturated solution contains as much solute as can dissolve under the stated conditions.

explain.title: Solubility depends on the substance and temperature
explain.body: Different compounds dissolve to different extents because their particles interact differently with water. The solubility of most solids increases as temperature rises; the solubility of gases generally decreases.

explain.title: Crystallization can purify a solid
explain.body: A substance such as potassium nitrate can be dissolved in hot water, and the solution can be cooled to form crystals. Filtering, washing and drying the crystals separates the purified solid from soluble impurities.

explain.title: Structure explains useful properties
explain.body: Graphite feels slippery because its layers slide over one another, while a diamond's high refractive index contributes to its brilliance. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms and is useful in electronics because of its electrical properties.

mistakes: Do not confuse plasma with an ordinary gas: plasma contains ionized particles.
Do not call every mixture a solution; suspensions and colloids have dispersed particles.
When defining solubility, include the temperature and the saturated-solution condition.
Do not say all solutes respond to heating in the same way: most solids become more soluble, while gases generally become less soluble.
For crystallization, do not cool before dissolving the impure solid in hot water and filtering the solution.
Do not describe graphene as many layers; it is a single layer, while graphite consists of stacked layers.
When comparing coal with diamond, distinguish impure amorphous coal from crystalline diamond.
In branch questions, choose the branch by the focus of the topic, not just by the name of a substance.

notes.title: What is Chemistry and why are there branches?
notes.answer: Chemistry studies substances, their properties, composition and structure, and changes in matter. Its branches focus on different aspects of this wide subject.
notes.explanation: Chemistry has several branches so scientists can focus on different kinds of substances and questions. For example, analytical chemistry identifies and measures components in a sample, while environmental chemistry studies chemical effects in air, soil and water. Nuclear chemistry focuses on changes in atomic nuclei.
notes.simple: Different chemistry branches are like different study areas: each one focuses on a particular kind of chemical question.
examples: Finding the components of a lunar sample: analytical chemistry.
Studying pollution caused by chemicals: environmental chemistry.
steps: Read what is being studied or measured.
Match it to the branch that focuses on that subject.
For a sample's components or concentrations, choose analytical chemistry.
notes.checkQuestion: Which branch deals with the separation, identification and measurement of components in a material?

notes.title: States of Matter
notes.answer: Matter can exist as a solid, liquid, gas or plasma, as well as in less commonly encountered states.
notes.explanation: Matter occurs in different states. The particle arrangement, distance between particles and strength of attractions explain how solids, liquids, gases and plasma behave.
notes.simple: Think of particles as tiny pieces. In a solid they are tightly packed, in a liquid they stay close but move around, and in a gas they are far apart.
examples: Ice is a solid: its particles are closely packed and stay around fixed positions.
Air is a gas: its particles are far apart, so it is easy to compress.
steps: Compare how close the particles are.
Compare how freely the particles can move.
Use the particle arrangement and attractions to explain the state’s properties.
notes.checkAnswer: Gases have particles that are very widely apart, no order whatsoever and very weak intermolecular forces.

notes.title: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
notes.answer: An element has one kind of atom; a compound has different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains more than one type of element or compound mixed in any ratio.
notes.explanation: Matter may be an element, a compound, or a mixture. An element has one kind of atom; a compound contains different elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains substances mixed in any ratio.
notes.simple: Think of the three types this way: an element has one kind of atom, a compound has different elements chemically joined, and a mixture has substances physically mixed together.
examples: Salt water is a homogeneous mixture because its concentration is uniform throughout.
A sample of rock is a heterogeneous mixture because its constituents are not present in the same concentration throughout.
steps: Check whether the sample contains one kind of atom, different elements chemically combined, or substances mixed together.
For a mixture, check whether its composition is uniform throughout.
Call a mixture homogeneous if uniform, and heterogeneous if not uniform.
notes.checkQuestion: What makes a compound different from a mixture?
notes.checkAnswer: A compound is a pure substance made up of two or more different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

notes.title: Allotropic Forms of Substances
notes.answer: Allotropic forms are different structural forms of the same element.
notes.explanation: Allotropy is when an element exists in different structural forms. The forms can have different properties. Carbon has diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene as its main allotropic forms; sulphur has rhombic and monoclinic forms.
notes.simple: One element can have different forms because its atoms are arranged differently. These forms may behave differently.
examples: Carbon: diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene
steps: Identify the element.
Name the different structural forms in which it exists.
Remember that these forms may have different properties.

notes.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
notes.answer: A compound has chemically combined elements in a fixed ratio; a mixture has components that are not chemically bound together.
notes.explanation: Elements, compounds and mixtures differ in what they contain and whether their particles are chemically joined. Elements contain one kind of atom; compounds contain elements chemically combined in fixed ratios; mixtures contain substances mixed without chemical bonding.
notes.simple: An element has one kind of atom. A compound has different elements chemically joined. A mixture has substances together but not chemically joined.
examples: Water (H₂O) is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Salt water is a mixture: salt and water are mixed, and the salt can be separated by physical methods.
steps: Check whether the sample contains one kind of atom or more than one substance.
If different elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio, it is a compound.
If substances are mixed without chemical bonding and can be separated physically, it is a mixture.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one key difference between a compound and a mixture?
notes.checkAnswer: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture contains components that are not chemically bound together.

notes.title: Telling solutions, colloids and suspensions apart
notes.answer: A true solution has particles that are not visible and pass through filter paper. A colloid has particles that do not settle and pass through filter paper. A suspension has visible particles that settle and are caught by filter paper.
notes.explanation: A true solution has solute particles completely mixed into the solvent. Colloidal particles are bigger than true-solution particles, but are too small to see with the naked eye. Suspension particles can be seen, settle if left standing, and are caught by filter paper.
notes.simple: Think about what happens when you leave a mixture standing or pour it through a filter. These clues help you tell the three mixtures apart.
examples: Starch solution is a colloidal solution.
A mixture of chalk in water is a suspension.
steps: Check whether the particles can be seen with the naked eye.
Leave the mixture standing: suspension particles settle, but colloidal particles do not.
Filter it: true-solution and colloidal particles pass through filter paper; suspension particles are left as residue.
notes.checkQuestion: Which kind of mixture has particles that settle on standing and can be collected on filter paper?
notes.checkAnswer: A suspension: its particles can be seen, settle on standing, and are caught by filter paper.

notes.title: Unsaturated and Saturated Solutions
notes.answer: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute; a saturated solution contains the maximum amount that can dissolve at that temperature.
notes.explanation: A solution is unsaturated if it can still dissolve more solute at a particular temperature. It is saturated when it has dissolved the maximum amount of solute possible in a particular amount of solvent at that temperature.
notes.simple: Unsaturated means more solute can dissolve. Saturated means no more can dissolve at that temperature.
examples: Sugar dissolves in water, and more sugar can still dissolve: the solution is unsaturated.
At 20°C, 36 g of sodium chloride dissolves in 100 g of water to make a saturated solution.
steps: Check whether more solute can dissolve at the same temperature.
If more can dissolve, the solution is unsaturated.
If the maximum amount has dissolved, the solution is saturated.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the difference between an unsaturated solution and a saturated solution?
notes.checkAnswer: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at that temperature; a saturated solution has dissolved the maximum amount.

notes.title: Temperature and solubility
notes.answer: The solubility of a gas in water generally decreases when the temperature increases.
notes.explanation: Temperature affects different solutes in different ways. Many solids dissolve better in warmer water, but some substances change very little or become less soluble. Gases generally become less soluble as water gets warmer.
notes.simple: Heating often lets water dissolve more solid, but not always. It usually makes water hold less gas.
examples: KNO₃ becomes much more soluble as temperature increases.
NaCl solubility changes very little with temperature.
steps: Remember the definition: solubility is measured for 100g of solvent at a particular temperature.
Check the substance: different solutes respond differently to temperature.
For many solids, heating increases solubility; for some, it changes little or decreases.
For gases, solubility in water generally decreases as temperature increases.
notes.checkQuestion: What usually happens to the solubility of a gas in water when the temperature increases?
notes.checkAnswer: Most solid solutes become more soluble as temperature rises, but this is not a rule for every substance. Gases generally become less soluble.

notes.title: States of Matter and Phase Changes
notes.answer: Matter in the Sun exists in the plasma state.
notes.explanation: Matter can be classified by its physical state and by whether it is a pure substance or a mixture. Chemistry is divided into branches so different kinds of substances, reactions and problems can be studied more easily. Temperature affects the solubility of many substances, and cooling a hot saturated solution can produce crystals.
notes.simple: Chemistry studies matter and its changes. Different branches focus on different kinds of matter and questions. Substances can have different structures and properties, and solubility often changes when temperature changes.
examples: Cooling a hot saturated potassium nitrate solution can produce potassium nitrate crystals.
steps: Identify the type of matter or process in the question.
Recall the relevant definition or property.
Apply it to the substance or example given.

written.text: Q1.1. Preparation of solutions leads to an important process in chemistry which enables us to purify a compound through crystallization. Describe a process in which potassium nitrate is purified by crystallizing it in water.
